analysis.one_liner: Loosens bank capital rules for 18 months to push banks to lend more to businesses and consumers.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in August 1993, sent to four House Banking subcommittees, and never got a hearing, a vote, or a floor appearance before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred federal banking regulators from requiring banks and thrifts to hold more than 3 cents of capital per dollar of assets for 18 months, so banks could lend more to small businesses and consumers. It also would have required regulators to soften real estate lending rules that limit credit, let appraisers licensed in one state work in others, created an appeals process for banks and borrowers who disagree with regulator decisions, coordinated bank examinations, and ordered studies and reports on capital rules and lending costs. It sat in committee and died when the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks and savings institutions that were adequately capitalized but constrained by the leverage rule, which could lend more with the same capital. Small businesses, homebuyers, and consumers would gain if lending actually expanded. Appraisers could work across state lines. Borrowers in good standing would get a new right to appeal when a bank cancels or cuts their credit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Adequately capitalized banks and their borrowers

how_it_helps.text: For 18 months, regulators could not enforce a leverage rule requiring adequately capitalized institutions to hold tangible equity above 3% of total assets, freeing capital for lending [S2][S3].

Regulators would have to consider and minimize the impact of real estate lending standards on credit for small business, residential, and agricultural borrowers and in low- and moderate-income communities [S2][S3].
Borrowers who were in full compliance with a loan could appeal to a new independent appellate process if a bank cancelled a loan, cut a credit line, or changed terms substantially against them [S3].
Banks would have to report the number of loans under $1 million, loans to small businesses, minority-owned businesses, and start-ups, making small-business lending visible [S2][S3].
The Federal Reserve and HUD would study how to streamline mortgage, small business, and consumer lending to reduce consumer cost and delay [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If a bank with a thin 3% capital cushion failed, losses would fall on the deposit insurance fund, which taxpayers backstop — the same dynamic that produced the savings-and-loan bailout a few years earlier. Regulators would lose their main lever to force weak banks to shore up. Banks would also bear reporting costs for the new loan disclosures.
analysis.who_pays_short: The deposit insurance fund and ultimately taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Freezing the leverage limit at 3% for adequately capitalized banks removes the simplest safety cushion; the bill's only guard is an exception for institutions judged to lack loan loss reserves or to be operating unsafely, which relies on regulators' discretion [S3].
Thinly capitalized banks that fail impose losses on the deposit insurance fund, and the bill would allow undercapitalized banks to sell credit card receivables with FDIC waiver protections [S2][S3].

Whether easier capital rules actually translate into more small business and consumer lending was unproven; the bill itself orders a Treasury report on how capital standards affect credit availability, acknowledging the question was open [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The goal — more lending to small businesses and ordinary borrowers after a credit crunch — was real, and some pieces (borrower appeal rights, loan disclosures, coordinated exams) are modest consumer wins. But the centerpiece, suspending the leverage rule, trades a proven safety measure for hoped-for lending, and the deposit insurance fund absorbs the downside if it fails. The bill asks taxpayers to backstop the risk while the upside accrues to bank shareholders and borrowers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Banking Committee, split among four subcommittees, and died there without a hearing or vote when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Joseph P. Kennedy II introduced the bill on August 6, 1993, with one Democratic cosponsor [S1][S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs on the day of introduction [S5].

On August 16, 1993, it was referred to four subcommittees: Consumer Credit and Insurance; Housing and Community Development; Economic Growth and Credit Formation; and Financial Institutions Supervision, Regulation and Deposit Insurance [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never left committee and received no floor vote before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banking regulators and the deposit insurance fund kept the stricter capital rules in place; banks did not get the capital relief they sought, and taxpayers avoided the added failure risk.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Regulators and the deposit insurance fund

for.name: Rep. Joseph P. Kennedy II
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Business and Consumer Lending Stimulus Act on August 6, 1993.

against.name: House Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, referred it to four subcommittees, and took no further action — no markup, no hearing, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor and never advanced far enough for a vote that would reveal a partisan split.

industries.note: The bill would have freed adequately capitalized banks from the leverage rule for 18 months, expanding lending capacity and profits, at the cost of a thinner safety cushion backed by the deposit insurance fund. Provisions coordinating examinations and adding regulatory appeals would also ease regulatory burdens on banks [S2][S3].

The bill directs the Appraisal Subcommittee to push states toward reciprocity, letting an appraiser licensed in one state work in others, and bars excessive fees for temporary practice — more work for appraisers and, in principle, faster cheaper appraisals for homebuyers [S3].

The bill lets the FDIC waive its right to repudiate credit card receivable sales by undercapitalized banks and protects customer lists in such sales, making it easier to package and sell card portfolios [S2][S3].
The bill's stated purpose is expanding credit to small and medium-sized businesses and consumers, and it adds borrower appeal rights and new disclosures on small business lending [S2][S3].
